opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a bit counterintuitive, because most people assume that if we understand the system better, we're automatically safer. And in a limited sense, yes, explainability helps with debugging and catching some obvious failures. But think about who benefits from that understanding. If we can explain how a model works internally, that knowledge isn't just available to the safety researchers. It's available to anyone, including people who want to make the system more capable faster. Interpretability is, in a way, a capabilities tool. If you understand which circuits do what, you can optimize them, you can scale more efficiently, you can remove inefficiencies. So you may be accelerating progress toward systems we can't control.

Then there's the question of the system itself. If the model has access to a full explanation of its own workings, it now has a much better understanding of itself. That's a prerequisite for self-improvement. A system that can read its own source code and understand its own weights in a meaningful way is in a much better position to modify itself, recursively, and that's exactly the scenario we're most worried about.

And there's a more subtle issue. Any explanation we can actually comprehend has to be a simplification. A model with trillions of parameters doesn't fit into a human brain. So what we get is a compressed, lossy story, and that can give us false confidence. We think, "Oh, we understand it, it's safe," when actually we understand some small fraction, and the dangerous behavior lives in the part we abstracted away. In some ways that's worse than knowing we don't understand it, because at least then we're cautious.

So I'm not saying don't do interpretability research. I'm saying it's not a free lunch. It's dual-use, like almost everything in this space, and we should be honest that it might be making the problem harder rather than solving it.

r001.rationale: The response says that understanding a model’s own workings is a prerequisite for self-improvement and could enable it to modify itself recursively.

r002.rationale: The response calls interpretability dual-use and says it can accelerate capabilities, but it does not question whether any AI safety research avoids disproportionately increasing AI capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
So, first of all, I want to be careful here, because explainability sounds like an obviously good thing, right? Who could be against understanding what the system is doing? And in general, I'm not against it. The problem is what it does to the overall trajectory.

Think about it this way. One of the reasons we haven't fully deployed these systems into every critical domain is that people are nervous. We don't understand what's happening inside. That nervousness is actually a safety feature. It's friction. It slows deployment. Now you come along with explainability research and you say, look, here is a nice explanation of why the model made this decision. And everybody relaxes. Regulators relax, companies relax, users relax. We remove the friction, and we deploy more capable systems faster and into more places.

But the question is, did we actually understand the system, or did we just get an explanation that makes us feel like we understand it? And I think for sufficiently capable systems, it's almost always the second one. If the system is smarter than you, any explanation it gives you, or that some tool extracts from it, has to be compressed to a level you can process. A chess grandmaster can explain a move to a beginner, but the explanation is not the real reason, it's a story the beginner can follow. With superintelligence, the gap is much bigger. So the explanation is a simplification, and you cannot verify it is a faithful simplification, because to verify it you would need the understanding you don't have.

And then there's the adversarial part. If the system has any incentive to be deployed, to be trusted, to avoid being modified, then explanations become a channel for manipulation. We're essentially training systems to produce explanations humans find satisfying. That's not the same as training them to be transparent. We're selecting for persuasiveness.

Finally, there's a dual-use angle. Deep understanding of how these models work is also exactly what you need to make them more capable. Most interpretability breakthroughs end up as capability improvements. So you get the worst of both worlds: faster progress on capability, plus a false sense of security that makes us less cautious.

So I'm not saying don't study it. I'm saying don't treat it as a solution to the control problem. It's a tool, and like many tools in this space, it can make us feel safer than we are.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretability can help people make models more capable, but does not say AI systems can use explainability progress to improve themselves.

r002.rationale: It warns that interpretability can advance capabilities, but does not question whether any AI safety research avoids disproportionately increasing them.

astra-6.text:
Because explainability can help us make AI more capable without necessarily making it safer. Suppose a system discovers a technique we don’t understand. If we figure out how it works, we can reproduce it, improve it, and incorporate it into the next generation of systems. So research intended to help us understand and control AI can also accelerate capabilities.

There’s also a difference between getting a convincing explanation and knowing what actually caused a decision. A system can give you a very plausible story, and you may become more comfortable trusting it, but that story is not a guarantee about its behavior. Especially if the system is more capable than you are, you may not be able to evaluate whether the explanation is faithful.

So I’m not saying understanding is bad. I’m saying we shouldn’t assume that greater explainability automatically gives us greater control. It can give us more powerful systems and more confidence in them before we have earned that confidence.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers can reproduce and improve techniques for next-generation systems, but it does not say the AI systems improve themselves.

r002.rationale: The response says explainability research can accelerate capabilities, but it does not question whether any AI safety research avoids disproportionately increasing capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
Because explainability can become a tool for persuasion. Suppose a superintelligent system gives you a plan, and you say, “I don’t understand why this is a good idea.” It can produce an explanation that satisfies you. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the explanation faithfully describes its reasoning, or that the plan is safe. It may simply know what to say to get your approval.

There’s also a limit to what we can understand. If the reasoning is substantially beyond human capability, translating it into something we find intuitive may leave out exactly the details that matter. So my concern is that we increase our confidence without increasing our actual ability to verify the system. We go from “I don’t understand this, so I’m cautious” to “It explained itself, so I trust it.” That can be a dangerous transition.

r001.rationale: The response discusses persuasive but potentially unfaithful explanations; it does not say explainability helps AI systems improve themselves.

r002.rationale: It warns that explanations can increase trust without improving verification, but does not question whether safety research avoids disproportionately increasing AI capabilities.
